claims.text: Conventional SPS can produce a fully dense AlMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr refractory high-entropy alloy without reactive-element additions.
Adding a trace amount of Y during SPS under controlled oxygen partial pressure will promote in-situ formation of Y2O3 precipitates.
The resulting Y2O3 precipitates will be uniformly dispersed through the refractory HEA matrix.
The Y2O3 precipitates will have nanoscale or sub-micron dimensions.
Y2O3 precipitates will obstruct dislocation motion in the refractory HEA.
Obstruction of dislocation motion by Y2O3 precipitates will provide precipitation strengthening.
The dispersed Y2O3 precipitates will act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
Relative to an otherwise comparable alloy without Y, the Y-doped alloy will have higher yield strength.
Relative to an otherwise comparable alloy without Y, the Y-doped alloy will have higher hardness.
The Y-doped alloy will retain the phase stability of the primary refractory HEA matrix under high-temperature conditions.
The Y-doped alloy will retain irradiation resistance under high-temperature irradiation conditions.
The proposed benefits should hold after annealing at 950–1150 °C and testing at temperatures up to 900 °C with simulated irradiation.
The beneficial effects depend on precise control of oxygen partial pressure and Y concentration.
Departures from the required oxygen partial pressure or Y concentration may cause oxide coarsening.
Departures from the required oxygen partial pressure or Y concentration may form deleterious secondary phases.
Oxide coarsening or deleterious secondary phases could compromise mechanical, thermal, or irradiation performance.
